title: Finite associative algebras and right comodules of their duals
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $E$ be a finite-dimensional associative unital $k$-algebra, not assumed commutative. Finite-dimensional means possessing a finite spanning set [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]; the multiplication is $k$-bilinear. Put $D=E^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(E,k)$ and use tensor products [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. There is a unique counital coassociative coalgebra structure on $D$ specified by
$$\langle\Delta d,a\otimes b\rangle=d(ab),\qquad\epsilon(d)=d(1_E)\quad(a,b\in E).$$
For any finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $M$, unital associative $k$-bilinear left $E$-actions correspond bijectively to linear maps $\rho:M\to M\otimes_kD$ satisfying $(\rho\otimes1)\rho=(1\otimes\Delta)\rho$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)\rho=1_M$. The action corresponding to $\rho$ is
$$a\cdot m=(1_M\otimes\operatorname{ev}_a)\rho(m),$$
and its inverse is $\rho(m)=\sum_j(a_j\cdot m)\otimes a_j^*$ for any finite basis $(a_j)$ of $E$ with dual basis $(a_j^*)$. These formulas are independent of that basis. A linear map is $E$-linear if and only if it commutes with the corresponding coactions. Thus they give an equivalence from finite-dimensional left $E$-modules to finite-dimensional right $D$-comodules which is the identity on underlying vector spaces and maps. The zero algebra and zero-dimensional spaces are included.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175, the paragraph following Lemma 9.35 on p.177 (opposite handedness), Example 9.36 and 9.41–9.42, printed pp.178–180.

proof.text: Choose a basis of each finite-dimensional vector space used below by [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free]. Such a basis is finite: take the union $J$ of the finite basis supports of a finite spanning family. Every vector then has support in $J$, whereas a basis vector outside $J$ would have its own coordinate equal to $1$, a contradiction. For $E$ write the basis as $(a_i)_{i\in I}$. Define $f_i:E\to k$ to be its coordinate maps. These are linear, $f_i(a_j)=\delta_{ij}$, and $a=\sum_i f_i(a)a_i$. Applying any $d\in E^*$ to this last equality gives $d=\sum_i d(a_i)f_i$. Thus $(f_i)$ is a basis of $D=E^*$, including when $I$ is empty.

source.place: Supporting basis input: Stacks Tag 09FN (fields-lemma-vector-space-is-free); finite support and coordinate argument supplied here.

proof.text: By [lem-sc-tensor-product-free-basis], the $f_i\otimes f_j$ form a basis of $D\otimes D$, and iterating the same statement gives a basis $f_i\otimes f_j\otimes f_h$ of the triple tensor product, with the canonical associator understood. Their coefficients are obtained by evaluation at $a_i\otimes a_j$ and $a_i\otimes a_j\otimes a_h$. Consequently those evaluations detect equality. For a finite-dimensional vector space $M$ with basis $(e_s)$, the same lemma gives a basis $(e_s\otimes f_i)$ of $M\otimes D$; hence every $z\in M\otimes D$ has the unique expression $z=\sum_i z_i\otimes f_i$, where $z_i=(1_M\otimes\operatorname{ev}_{a_i})z$. Repeating this argument gives equality detection in $M\otimes D\otimes D$ by $1_M\otimes\operatorname{ev}_{a_i}\otimes\operatorname{ev}_{a_j}$. The tensor maps and associator here are defined on pure tensors by the universal property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]; inverse associators compose to the identity on pure tensors, which generate.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175: tensor-dual pairing and comodule coefficient identities; explicit finite-basis equality detection.

proof.text: Let $\mu:E\otimes E\to E$ be induced by multiplication using [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-free-tensor-dual] to $E,E$, whose finite bases were established in Step 1. Its canonical isomorphism $\theta:D\otimes D\xrightarrow{\sim}(E\otimes E)^*$ sends $f\otimes g$ to $(a\otimes b\mapsto f(a)g(b))$. Define $\Delta(d)=\theta^{-1}(d\circ\mu)$ and $\epsilon(d)=d(1_E)$. Both maps are linear. Their required pairing formula follows directly from the formula for $\theta$; equivalently $\Delta(d)=\sum_{i,j}d(a_i a_j)f_i\otimes f_j$. Step 2 shows that the pairing formula determines $\Delta$ uniquely, while the displayed formula determines $\epsilon$. Thus their construction is independent of the chosen basis.

source.place: §9(d), p.174: canonical tensor-dual map; paragraph after Lemma 9.35, p.177, and Example 9.36, p.178: dual of a finite algebra.

proof.text: Evaluate $(\Delta\otimes1)\Delta(d)$ on $a\otimes b\otimes c$: the result is $d((ab)c)$. Evaluating $(1\otimes\Delta)\Delta(d)$ gives $d(a(bc))$. Associativity in $E$ and the triple equality detection of Step 2 prove coassociativity. Evaluating $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta(d)$ at $a$ gives $d(1_Ea)=d(a)$, and evaluating $(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta(d)$ gives $d(a1_E)=d(a)$. Since the $a_i$ form a basis, these are the two counit identities. The uniqueness established in Step 3 therefore proves the asserted uniqueness of the coalgebra structure, without assuming that $E$ is commutative.

source.place: §9(d), p.174 and Example 9.36, p.178; agent verification by evaluating the transposed associativity and unit identities.

proof.text: Given a unital associative bilinear left action, define the linear map $\rho(m)=\sum_i(a_i\cdot m)\otimes f_i$. For every $a\in E$, contraction gives $\sum_i f_i(a)(a_i\cdot m)=a\cdot m$ by the basis expansion of $a$ and bilinearity. After contraction at $a,b$ on its two $D$ factors, $(\rho\otimes1)\rho(m)$ is $a\cdot(b\cdot m)$, whereas $(1\otimes\Delta)\rho(m)$ is $(ab)\cdot m$ by Step 3. Associativity of the action and Step 2 give the coassociativity identity for $\rho$. Its counit is $\sum_i f_i(1_E)(a_i\cdot m)=1_E\cdot m=m$. Thus the formula produces a right $D$-comodule. Notice the order $ab$: no opposite algebra or reversal of tensor factors is being inserted.

source.place: Example 9.36, p.178, and 9.42, p.180; expanded verification of the right-comodule convention.

proof.text: Conversely let $\rho:M\to M\otimes D$ be a right coaction. Define $a\cdot m=(1_M\otimes\operatorname{ev}_a)\rho(m)$. This is linear in $m$ because $\rho$ and contraction are linear, and linear in $a$ because $d\mapsto d(a)$ depends linearly on $a$. Since $\operatorname{ev}_{1_E}=\epsilon$, the counit identity gives $1_E\cdot m=m$. Apply $1_M\otimes\operatorname{ev}_a\otimes\operatorname{ev}_b$ to $(\rho\otimes1)\rho(m)=(1\otimes\Delta)\rho(m)$. The left side becomes $a\cdot(b\cdot m)$ and the right side becomes $(ab)\cdot m$, by the defining pairing formula of $\Delta$. This proves precisely the required associative left action.

source.place: Example 9.36, p.178, and 9.42, p.180; expanded evaluation of the coaction axioms.

proof.text: Starting with an action, Step 5 already shows that recovering it from its coaction returns $a\cdot m$ for every $a,m$. Starting with $\rho$, its recovered action satisfies $a_i\cdot m=(1_M\otimes\operatorname{ev}_{a_i})\rho(m)$. The unique normal form in Step 2 therefore gives $\sum_i(a_i\cdot m)\otimes f_i=\rho(m)$. The two constructions are inverse bijections. The same normal-form uniqueness also proves basis independence of the action-to-coaction construction: for any other finite basis the resulting tensor has contraction $a\cdot m$ for every $a$, so equals the first tensor. The coaction-to-action formula has no choice of basis.

source.place: Example 9.36, p.178: canonical comodule structure; explicit inverse and basis-independence check.

proof.text: For linear $u:M\to N$, contract the difference $\rho_Nu-(u\otimes1_D)\rho_M$ at $a$. Its value on $m$ is $a\cdot u(m)-u(a\cdot m)$. If $u$ is colinear all these differences vanish, so $u$ is $E$-linear. If $u$ is $E$-linear they vanish for every basis vector $a_i$, and Step 2 detects that the difference of tensors is zero; hence $u$ is colinear. The two assignments on objects from Steps 5–7 therefore extend to functors by leaving every underlying linear map fixed. They preserve identities and compositions literally. Their composites recover each action and coaction by Step 7 and each morphism by construction, giving inverse functors and thus the claimed equivalence of finite-dimensional categories.

source.place: Example 9.36, p.178, and 9.42, p.180: equivalence with canonical comodule structure; explicit morphism calculation.

proof.text: All computations permit empty bases and zero sums. If $M=0$ the action and coaction are unique and all identities hold. If $E=0$, then $D=0$ and $\Delta,\epsilon$ are the unique zero maps; the coalgebra identities hold because $1_D=0$. For any $M$, a bilinear action of $E=0$ has $1_E\cdot m=0$, so is unital exactly when $M=0$. Likewise the sole map $M\to M\otimes0=0$ is counital exactly when $1_M=0$, equivalently $M=0$. Thus for nonzero $M$ both sets of structures are empty, and for zero $M$ both are singletons; the equivalence includes the stated degenerate cases.

source.place: Agent edge-case verification of Example 9.36, p.178, allowing the zero unital algebra and zero vector spaces.

proof_origin.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175 and 177–178, Example 9.36, and 9.41–9.42, pp.179–180. Milne states the dictionary; Q28 supplies the explicit finite-coordinate proof of every clause.
